summary: Israel votes, Iran hosts three US partners for talks, protests test France's ban, Machado returns to Venezuela, Ebola passes 10,000 cases, and Starlink becomes a war issue.

topics.heading: Israel votes today in its first election since the October 7 attack
topics.summary: Israelis are electing a new 120-seat Knesset, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu facing former army chief Gadi Eisenkot. Final polls showed neither camp reaching the 61 seats needed to govern; exit polls come when voting closes tonight.[^1][^2]

lead.title: Israel elections: Polls open as Netanyahu fights to retain power

alsoReported.title: Voters start casting ballots as polling stations open across Israel

article: Polls opened at 7 a.m. local time on Tuesday and close at 10 p.m. (4 p.m. in Toronto), with about 7.3 million people eligible to vote[^1][^2]. It is the first national election since the Hamas-led attack of October 7, 2023, and the war in Gaza that followed[^1]. Exit polls air when voting ends; the full count is due by October 30 and official results on November 4[^1].

Israelis vote for party lists, not individual candidates, and seats are shared out in proportion to votes. A party needs 3.25% of the vote to enter the Knesset, and a government needs the support of 61 of its 120 members, so every Israeli government is a coalition[^3]. Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister, leads a coalition of right-wing, far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties formed in 2022; Eisenkot leads a new party, Yashar[^1].

Final polls put Yashar ahead of Netanyahu's Likud, with Netanyahu's bloc projected at around 50 seats and neither side near 61[^1][^2]. Parties led by Palestinian citizens of Israel, who make up about 18% of eligible voters, are projected to win 14 to 16 seats, but both main camps have ruled out including them in a government[^1].

Security has dominated the campaign. Trump urged Israelis to vote for Netanyahu, calling him an "outstanding Warrior"[^6]. Iran's foreign ministry said the result "makes no difference" to Tehran[^7]. Turnout is projected at 60 to 70%, up from 53% in 2022, and Palestinian-majority towns reported high early turnout[^1].

What next: within seven days of official results, President Isaac Herzog picks the lawmaker most likely to form a coalition, who then has 28 days, with a possible 14-day extension[^3]. If no one succeeds, Israel could face another election[^3]. My read: tonight's numbers will show who has the better chance, but the coalition bargaining that follows may matter more, for Gaza, Iran policy and Israel's ties with Washington.

topics.heading: Iran hosts Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani officials as Houthi missiles target Saudi Arabia
topics.summary: Saudi Arabia's defence minister, Pakistan's army chief and Turkey's intelligence chief held talks in Tehran on Monday. They agreed to keep talking but announced no measures, while the Saudi-led coalition said it shot down more Houthi missiles and drones.[^4][^5]

lead.title: Iran hails 'very good' talks with Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Türkiye amid fresh Houthi attacks

alsoReported.title: Iran says 4-nation talks back regional security free of outside interference
Iran War Updates: Tehran shrugs off Trump's attack threats, says diplomacy ongoing as oil prices stay high

article: On Monday, Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, Pakistani army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin met Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, in Tehran, and later President Masoud Pezeshkian[^4]. The three visitors' countries signed a defence pact in August that treats an attack on one as an attack on all; it was their first joint meeting with Iran[^4]. A joint statement said only that the four would keep talking[^4].

Background: the war began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February, and Iranian attacks have since hit infrastructure in Gulf states[^4]. A Pakistan-brokered interim deal in June was meant to reopen the Strait of Hormuz to shipping, but it fell apart as attacks resumed[^4]. Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, was around $116 a barrel early Tuesday[^7].

The fighting continued around the talks. The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted three ballistic missiles aimed at Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province early Tuesday, after the Houthis, an Iran-aligned group in Yemen, said they had targeted Riyadh's airport and oil pumping stations[^4][^7]. CNN reported, citing two US officials, that US forces could begin major operations against Iran within 96 hours of an order, though no decision has been made[^6].

Why it matters: Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan are US partners, so a regional channel to Tehran could become a route to a deal, or a sign that the region is planning its own security arrangements. My read: with no concrete steps announced, it is too early to call this a breakthrough.
topics.differences: Rezaei said the visits show US threats are not working and that the region's security should be kept free of outside interference[^5]. Saudi Arabia described the aim as finding ways to de-escalate[^4]. Trump asked publicly whether to "make a deal" or "finish them off"[^7], and an Iranian official said the US must meet seven conditions before new talks[^6].

topics.heading: France arrests more than 1,300 people as cost-of-living protests defy a ban
topics.summary: Hundreds of thousands marched across France on Saturday over living costs, schools and public services. Police made 1,314 arrests after President Macron banned non-union protests; similar youth-led protests have spread to Italy, Belgium, Spain and Albania.[^8][^9]

lead.title: Over 1,300 people arrested during protests in France

alsoReported.title: From arrests to crackdowns, how Europe's leaders are responding as protests rock the continent

article: France's interior ministry said police arrested 1,314 people during Saturday's protests and that 53 officers were hurt[^8]. Turnout estimates ranged from 410,000 (authorities) to 800,000 (the CGT union), and 70,000 police and other security staff were deployed[^8]. A week earlier, rioting had led to 2,700 arrests[^8].

The unrest began in mid-September with student protests over school conditions[^9]. Protesters' demands now include relief from the cost of living, protection of public services and "fiscal and social justice"[^8]. Macron banned demonstrations not organised by unions, calling them "illegitimate", and the government ordered police to keep marches out of city centres; many protesters see this as an attack on the right to protest[^8].

Most union-organised marches were peaceful, but clashes broke out later in Paris, Lyon, Lille, Toulouse and Nantes, where police used tear gas and water cannon[^9]. Police responded to 75 fires, and 24 shops were looted[^8].

The protests have spread, each with local grievances. In Italy, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni sent 500 extra soldiers to Milan; Belgium reported nearly 200 arrests in protests over education cuts; Barcelona police arrested 128 people; and in Albania, student protests turned into calls for Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign[^9].

Why it matters: France votes for a new president in April and May. Marine Le Pen, who leads first-round polls with 32 to 34% according to Ipsos, accuses the government of being soft on violent protesters[^8]. What next: Yellow Vest groups have called for more protests on October 31[^8]. My read: whether the bans calm things or add a new grievance will shape that campaign.
topics.differences: Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez blamed "500 rioters" for the Paris clashes, and a French intelligence report cited by media blamed far-left groups[^8][^9]. Protesters say the ban is the bigger threat to democracy[^8]. Trump blamed immigration; Macron called such foreign comments "unacceptable and even stupid"[^9].

topics.heading: María Corina Machado returns to Venezuela and demands an election date
topics.summary: Venezuela's best-known opposition leader came home on Sunday after more than ten months in exile, greeted by crowds of supporters. No presidential election has been scheduled since US forces removed Nicolás Maduro in January.[^10][^11]

lead.title: Exiled Opposition Leader María Corina Machado Returns to Venezuela

alsoReported.title: Venezuela opposition leader Machado returns after months in exile

article: María Corina Machado, who won the 2025 Nobel Peace Prize, announced on Sunday that she was back in Venezuela, posting "I am here. With you."[^10] The New York Times reported she crossed from Colombia, according to TIME[^10]. AP reporters saw supporters cheer her in a church in Lara state as she headed toward Caracas[^11]. Her party says she made seven earlier attempts to return[^11].

Background: in 2024 the government barred Machado from running for president. Edmundo González ran in her place, and AP says credible evidence shows he won by more than two to one, but the ruling-party-controlled electoral council declared Maduro the winner[^11]. In January, US forces captured Maduro in Caracas and took him to New York on drug charges, which he denies[^11]. His deputy, Delcy Rodríguez, has run the country since; her initial 90-day mandate was never formally extended[^10][^11].

Machado wants elections by July 2027 and says she will run[^10]. Talks between the government, a different US-backed opposition group and Washington ended a third round this month without an election schedule[^10]. Secretary of State Marco Rubio says Venezuela must first stabilise its economy and rebuild institutions such as its courts and electoral council[^11]. Trump said he did not know about her return but hoped she would be safe[^11].

What next: the key questions are whether the interim government lets her campaign freely and whether her return speeds up an election date. My read: her popularity gives her leverage, but she is outside the talks that are deciding the timetable.
topics.differences: Opposition activists say the government blocked her return, which Venezuelan authorities deny[^11]. US officials deny holding her back but say they advised against returning for safety reasons[^11]. Critics say Washington has put business, including an oil deal, ahead of a democratic transition; the US says stability must come first[^10].

topics.heading: Congo's Ebola outbreak passes 10,000 confirmed cases
topics.summary: Congo's health ministry says confirmed cases have reached 10,060, making this the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record. It is caused by the rare Bundibugyo strain, for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment.[^12][^13]

lead.title: Congo's Ebola outbreak tops 10,000 cases as authorities race to slow the spread in African countries

alsoReported.title: DR Congo: Ebola responders under pressure as outbreak expands

article: Congo's Ministry of Health reported 10,060 confirmed cases, and AP says nearly half of those confirmed have died[^12]. UN News reported more than 4,600 deaths as of last week[^13]. The outbreak, declared in May, now covers 66 health zones in eight provinces, up from three zones at the start, with Ituri province at its centre[^12].

The outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, a rare type of Ebola[^12]. Unlike the more common Zaire type, it has no approved vaccine or treatment; researchers are testing whether the existing Ervebo vaccine gives any cross-protection, but there is no data yet[^13]. Cases have also been confirmed in Uganda, Kenya, Nigeria and France[^13].

The warning signs are in the tracing. About 80% of new cases are not linked to known contacts, which means the virus is spreading in ways health teams cannot see; Africa CDC says at least 95% should be before an outbreak is under control[^12]. Armed conflict, poor roads, mistrust and unpaid health workers slow the response, and a nurse was killed in Tshopo province[^12].

AP calls it the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history and the deadliest in Congo's history; for comparison, the 2014-2016 West Africa epidemic, the largest before this one, had more than 28,000 cases[^12]. At least half of deaths have been among people never admitted to a treatment centre[^12].

Why it matters: the outbreak is also hurting other care. AP reports maternal deaths have doubled in some provinces as pregnant women avoid hospitals, and routine child vaccinations have been disrupted[^12]. What next: watch whether the share of cases from known contacts rises, and whether vaccine trial results arrive.

topics.heading: Musk says SpaceX throttled Ukraine's Starlink; Kyiv disputes his reason
topics.summary: Elon Musk said SpaceX limited Starlink in Ukraine because its military used it for offensive drone strikes. Ukraine says long-standing limits made that impossible, and service was restored on Saturday after a week of disruption.[^14][^15]

lead.title: Ukraine disputes Elon Musk's claim that its military violated Starlink's terms of service

alsoReported.title: Ukraine's Starlink restored as Elon Musk claims Kyiv violated terms of service 'to kill people'

article: On Saturday, Elon Musk said SpaceX had throttled Starlink in Ukraine because the military broke its terms of service by using it "for offensive drone strikes to kill people", adding that "that loophole was closed last week"[^14]. Ukraine's Ministry of Defence said the same day that broader access had been restored after more than a week of speed limits[^15].

Starlink is SpaceX's satellite internet service, and Starshield is its military version, which AP describes as the backbone of Ukraine's drone operations and communications[^14]. During the restrictions, commanders reported lost drones and disrupted missions, including air defence against daily Russian attacks[^14]. A source told Fox News that Ukraine got no warning, although its service is contracted through the US government until May 2027[^15].

The timing mattered. Zelenskyy said that in the past week alone Russia launched nearly 2,300 attack drones, about 1,600 guided bombs and 48 missiles at Ukraine, and he asked Western allies to speed up deliveries of interceptors[^14]. Musk, for his part, said Starlink cannot be jammed and that the front line "would collapse immediately" without it[^15].

Who decided is still unclear. Musk says changes to Starshield are up to the US government[^14][^15]. Trump says he did not make the call, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and War Secretary Pete Hegseth deny the government caused the slowdown, and Vice President JD Vance has hinted at coordination with Musk[^14][^15].

Why it matters: a private company's network has become part of how a war is fought, and Zelenskyy said the US had "betrayed" him[^15]. The dispute comes as Russia agreed to resume three-way talks next month[^14]. My read: expect European governments to push harder for their own satellite systems.
topics.differences: Musk says Ukraine used Starlink for offensive strikes[^14]. Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to Zelenskyy, says civilian Starlink on drones was already capped at 70 to 90 km/h inside Ukraine and did not work in Russia, so deep strikes were "physically" impossible[^14].

question.text: Ukraine's drones depend partly on satellites run by one private company, and its owner can change how they work. If governments decide they can no longer rely on a single private provider for something this important, what else might change as a result, and who would pay for it?
